title: Histograms: Frequency Density and Unequal Class Widths
description: Histograms with unequal class widths: class width, frequency density, area represents frequency, reading frequencies back, and the tallest-bar trap for IGCSE Maths 0580 Extended.

notes.heading: What a Histogram Is
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A histogram looks like a bar chart, but the data is continuous and grouped into class intervals, and the **area** of each bar represents the frequency. The horizontal axis is the variable itself (measured continuously), and the vertical axis is frequency density.

🔑 How it works
In a normal bar chart the height shows the frequency. In a histogram the bars can have different widths, so height alone would lie — instead the height is adjusted so that width × height always equals the frequency.

💡 Worked Example 1
If one class is $0 < t \le 10$ and the next is $10 < t \le 40$, the second bar is three times as wide as the first, so its height must be scaled down for the areas to tell the truth about frequencies.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the two charts: bar charts have equal-width bars for discrete categories, histograms have possibly unequal widths for continuous data.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Area of bar = frequency.
• Vertical axis label on a histogram: frequency density.

✅ Check
A histogram for times taken, grouped as $0 < t \le 10$, $10 < t \le 40$, uses unequal widths.

notes.heading: Class Width
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The class width is the upper class boundary minus the lower class boundary.

$$\text{class width} = \text{upper boundary} - \text{lower boundary}$$

🔑 How it works
Read each class interval from the boundary numbers printed on the horizontal axis; subtract to get the width.

💡 Worked Example 1
The class $20 < h \le 50$ has width $50 - 20 = 30$.

💡 Worked Example 2
The class $0 < t \le 10$ has width $10 - 0 = 10$. So a histogram with classes $0 < t \le 10$ and $10 < t \le 40$ has bars of width 10 and width 30 — unequal.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Counting class limits wrongly, or subtracting the previous lower boundary instead of the class's own boundaries. Each class uses its own pair of numbers.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Width comes from the axis boundaries, never from the frequency.
• Unequal class widths are exactly why frequency density is needed.

✅ Check
The class $12 < x \le 20$ has width 8.

notes.heading: Frequency Density: The Height of a Bar
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Frequency density is the frequency per single unit of class width:

$$\text{frequency density} = \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$$

🔑 How it works
Divide each class's frequency by its own class width. That result is the height of the bar to draw.

💡 Worked Example 1
A class of width 3 has frequency 24, so frequency density $= 24 \div 3 = 8$.

💡 Worked Example 2
A class of width 6 has frequency 15, so frequency density $= 15 \div 6 = 2.5$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing density as width ÷ frequency — it is frequency ÷ width. A density is a rate: 'how many data values per one unit along the axis'.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Density can be a decimal; that is fine.
• Equal widths would give densities proportional to frequencies — which is why simple bar charts can skip the conversion.

✅ Check
Frequency 40 in a class of width 10 gives a density of 4.

notes.heading: Drawing a Histogram from a Table
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Give each class its width, divide frequency by width for the height, then draw one bar per class sitting exactly on its interval with no gaps.

💡 Worked Example
Table: $0 < w \le 10$, frequency 40; $10 < w \le 30$, frequency 50; $30 < w \le 35$, frequency 20.

Widths are 10, 20 and 5, so the densities are $40 \div 10 = 4$, $50 \div 20 = 2.5$ and $20 \div 5 = 4$. Draw bars of height 4, 2.5 and 4 over those intervals.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Leaving gaps between bars. Histogram bars touch because the variable is continuous; gaps belong to bar charts of discrete categories.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One width, one division per class.
• Label axes: variable along the bottom, frequency density up the side.

✅ Check
The three bars above have areas $10 \times 4 = 40$, $20 \times 2.5 = 50$ and $5 \times 4 = 20$ — the frequencies.

notes.heading: Reading Frequencies Back from a Histogram
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Because area represents frequency, recovering a frequency means multiplying the bar's height by its width:

$$\text{frequency} = \text{height} \times \text{class width}$$

🔑 How it works
Take the density from the vertical axis and the width from the horizontal axis boundaries, and multiply.

💡 Worked Example 1
A bar covering $10 < t \le 30$ has height 2.5. Width $= 20$, so frequency $= 2.5 \times 20 = 50$.

💡 Worked Example 2
To find the total number of data values, work out each bar's area and add: $40 + 50 + 20 = 110$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading the height off the vertical axis and calling it the frequency. It is only the frequency when the width is exactly 1.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Height × width = frequency, always.
• Total frequency = sum of all bar areas.

✅ Check
A bar of height 3 covering $0 < d \le 28$ has frequency $3 \times 28 = 84$.

notes.heading: The Tallest-Bar Trap
notes.body:
📌 Definition
On a histogram the tallest bar is the most **dense** class, not necessarily the class with the most data values.

🔑 How it works
Compare classes by area (height × width), never by height alone, whenever the widths differ.

💡 Worked Example
Class $0 < t \le 10$ has height 5: area $5 \times 10 = 50$. Class $10 < t \le 40$ has height 2: area $2 \times 30 = 60$. The shorter bar actually contains more data — 60 values against 50.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'the tallest bar is the most popular'. That is only safe when all bars share one width.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Equal widths: heights rank the frequencies correctly.
• Unequal widths: only areas rank them.

✅ Check
Width 10, height 5 versus width 30, height 2: the second class wins 60 to 50.

notes.heading: Comparing Distributions by Shape
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The overall shape of a histogram tells you how the data is spread. A long tail stretching to the right (towards the larger values) is called positive skew; a long tail to the left is negative skew.

🔑 How it works
Look at where the tall, wide bars sit. If most of the area — hence most of the data — is on the left and a thin tail trails right, the values are mostly low with a few high outliers.

💡 Worked Example 1
A histogram of 100 swimmers' reaction times has bars getting shorter to the right with a long right tail. Most swimmers took a short time, a few took much longer; the mean is pulled above the typical value.

💡 Worked Example 2
Two histograms of the same variable: A piles its area at the low end with a right tail, B is roughly symmetric. A has more values below the middle than B.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reading skew from the tallest bar alone — shape uses the whole distribution of area.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Right tail → positive skew → most values low.
• Left tail → negative skew → most values high.

✅ Check
Long tail to the right means most data values sit at the low end.

flashcards.definition: A chart for continuous grouped data where the area of each bar represents the frequency.
flashcards.example: Times grouped as 0 < t ≤ 10 and 10 < t ≤ 40 are drawn as a histogram.

flashcards.definition: Upper class boundary minus lower class boundary.
Frequency divided by class width — the height of a histogram bar.
Bar height × bar width equals the class frequency.

flashcards.term: Why the vertical axis is frequency density
flashcards.definition: Unequal widths mean height alone would mislead; density rescales so areas match frequencies.
flashcards.example: A class of width 30 with frequency 60 draws at height 2, not 60.

flashcards.definition: Find the bar's area: multiply its height by its class width.
flashcards.example: Height 3 across 0 < d ≤ 28 gives 84 data values.

flashcards.definition: With unequal widths the tallest bar is the densest class, not the most frequent one.
flashcards.example: Width 10 height 5 (area 50) loses to width 30 height 2 (area 60).

flashcards.definition: Add the areas of all the bars.
A long tail to the right: most values sit at the low end with a few high ones.
flashcards.example: Reaction times: most swimmers fast, a few very slow.

flashcards.definition: A long tail to the left: most values sit at the high end with a few low ones.
flashcards.example: Exam marks piled near full marks with a handful of very low ones.

flashcards.definition: Treat every class separately: its own width, its own density division.
flashcards.example: Widths 10, 20, 5 need three separate frequency ÷ width calculations.

flashcards.definition: Data values per one unit of the variable on the horizontal axis.
flashcards.example: Density 4 for lengths in cm means 4 values per centimetre of class.

questions.stem: A class in a histogram is $20 < h \le 50$. What is its class width?
questions.explanation: Width = upper boundary − lower boundary = $50 - 20 = 30$. The option 70 adds the boundaries instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: A class has frequency 24 and class width 3. What is the frequency density?
questions.explanation: Density = frequency ÷ width = $24 \div 3 = 8$. The option 72 multiplies instead of dividing; 6 swaps the numbers.

questions.stem: A class has frequency 15 and class width 6. What is the frequency density?
questions.explanation: $15 \div 6 = 2.5$. A density may be a decimal; 0.4 is width ÷ frequency, the division the wrong way round.

questions.stem: In a histogram, what does the area of each bar represent?
questions.explanation: Area = frequency, which is why the vertical axis is frequency density: height × width must come back to the class frequency.

questions.stem: The class $0 < t \le 10$ has frequency 40. What height is its bar on a histogram?
questions.explanation: Height = density = $40 \div 10 = 4$. The width here is 10, not 40 — do not divide by the frequency.

questions.stem: A bar covers the class $30 < m \le 45$ and has height 2. What is the frequency?
questions.explanation: Width = $45 - 30 = 15$, and frequency = height × width = $2 \times 15 = 30$. Reading 15 stops after finding the width.

questions.stem: A histogram has three bars: width 10 with height 4, width 20 with height 2.5, and width 10 with height 6. How many data values are there in total?
questions.explanation: Areas: $10 \times 4 = 40$, $20 \times 2.5 = 50$, $10 \times 6 = 60$. Total = $40 + 50 + 60 = 150$. Adding heights instead of areas gives 12.5 — meaningless here.

questions.stem: A histogram has a bar for $0 < t \le 10$ at height 5 and a bar for $10 < t \le 40$ at height 2. Which class contains more data values?
choices: They contain exactly the same number
It cannot be determined from the heights and widths
questions.explanation: Areas decide: $5 \times 10 = 50$ but $2 \times 30 = 60$. The shorter, wider class wins — the tallest-bar trap in action.

questions.stem: The class $12 < x \le 20$ has frequency 36. What is its frequency density?
questions.explanation: Width = $20 - 12 = 8$, density = $36 \div 8 = 4.5$. The option 4 divides $36 \div 8$ badly; 288 multiplies.

questions.stem: A histogram of 100 swimmers' times has bars that shrink towards the right with a long tail at the high end. Where do most swimmers' times lie?
choices: At the high end, in the tail
At the low end, away from the tail
Exactly in the middle of the range
questions.explanation: A right-hand tail (positive skew) means most of the area — hence most values — sits at the low end, with a few slow times stretching the tail.

questions.stem: Class $0 < d \le 15$ has frequency 45 and class $15 < d \le 45$ has frequency 120. What is the difference between their frequency densities?
questions.explanation: Densities: $45 \div 15 = 3$ and $120 \div 30 = 4$; the difference is $4 - 3 = 1$. The option 8 is 4 + 3; 45 compares frequencies, not densities.

questions.stem: A class has width 28 and frequency 84. What height must its bar have?
questions.explanation: Height = density = $84 \div 28 = 3$. Check: $3 \times 28 = 84$. The option 0.33 inverts the division; 2352 multiplies.

questions.stem: A histogram of 100 masses has a bar for $0 < m \le 10$ at height 4 and a bar for $10 < m \le 40$ at height 2. What percentage of the values are greater than 10?
questions.explanation: Values above 10: $2 \times 30 = 60$. Out of 100, that is 60%. The option 40% is the count below 10 ($4 \times 10$) read as a percentage of the wrong class.

questions.stem: A class $40 < d \le 48$ has a frequency density of 3.5. What is its frequency?
questions.explanation: Width = $48 - 40 = 8$, and frequency = density × width = $3.5 \times 8 = 28$. The option 6.5 adds instead of multiplying.

questions.stem: A histogram has bars of height 5 covering $0 < x \le 8$, height 2.5 covering $8 < x \le 28$, and height 4 covering $28 < x \le 33$. Which class holds the most data values?
choices: Cannot be determined without the frequencies
questions.explanation: Areas: $5 \times 8 = 40$, $2.5 \times 20 = 50$, $4 \times 5 = 20$. The middle class holds 50 — the *shortest* bar, because its width of 20 compensates.
